what_it_does: Chip designers and semiconductor process engineers need to work together tightly: designers need accurate models of how a new process technology behaves before it is fully finalized, and process engineers need fast feedback on whether their technology choices help or hurt circuit performance. The traditional bottleneck is that detailed circuit simulation (called SPICE simulation — a standard tool that numerically solves transistor equations) is slow, and the 'process design kit' (the rulebook and model files that describe a given manufacturing process) takes a long time to release. This paper replaces slow SPICE simulations with neural compact models — small neural networks trained to predict transistor behavior — which can be quickly re-tuned for new process variants via fine-tuning rather than retraining from scratch. It also recreates the conditions of a full design environment (things like layout-dependent parasitics — unwanted electrical effects from how wires are physically arranged — and process spread) using data interpolation tricks, so designers get realistic predictions without waiting for real silicon measurements.
